info.name: Portfolio API
info.description:
API tests for the backend of the Syed Waleed Ahmed portfolio (https://syedwaleedahmed.me).

The service accepts contact-form submissions and relays them as email through Resend. There is no database and no authentication.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/` | Root probe |
| `GET` | `/health` | Health check with server time |
| `POST` | `/api/contact` | Submit the contact form |

## Setup

1. Import this collection and one of the two environment files.
2. Select **Portfolio API - Local** (`http://localhost:5000`) or **Portfolio API - Production** (the live Render backend) from the environment dropdown.
3. Run requests individually, or use the Collection Runner for the whole suite.

`{{baseUrl}}` is the only variable. The collection carries a local default, so it still runs if no environment is selected.

## Before running against production

Only **POST /api/contact - Valid submission** sends a real email. Every other request stops before the mailer.

The backend is on Render's free tier and sleeps after inactivity, so the first request can take 30 to 60 seconds to cold-start.

## Notes

- `POST /api/contact` is rate-limited to 5 requests per IP per 15 minutes. Running the full collection uses several of those.
- Every request asserts status code and response shape with `pm.test()`, so the Runner reports real failures.
- Full API reference: `docs/api.md` in the repository.

item.name: Contact
item.description:
The contact endpoint and every documented failure path: validation, the body cap, the honeypot and the rate limiter.

Six of these requests consume rate-limit quota and the limit is 5 per IP per 15 minutes, so a full-folder run exhausts it by design. Their tests report a `429` as **skipped** rather than failed, since the limiter has its own request at the end of the folder. Restart the backend to clear the counter and get a full pass again.

exec: // This endpoint allows 5 requests / IP / 15 min, and a full
// collection run exceeds that. A 429 here means the window is
// exhausted, not that the behaviour under test broke - so report
// it as skipped and let the dedicated rate-limit request cover it.
pm.test('returns mailer error payload (503 unconfigured / 502 delivery failed)', () => {

request.description:
Submits a valid payload.

- `200` when the email sends. The response carries Resend's `id`.
- `503` if the mailer is unconfigured (`RESEND_API_KEY`, `EMAIL_FROM` or `EMAIL_TO` unset on the server).
- `502` if Resend rejects the send.

The test accepts all three, so the request passes against a backend running without mail credentials.

**This is the only request in the collection that sends a real email.** Every other request stops before the mailer and is safe to run against production.

request.description:
Fills the hidden `website` honeypot field.

The submission is dropped without sending, but answers with the same `200` and the same message a real send returns - a bot that could tell rejection from success would just retry without the field. The only tell is the absent `id`.

Safe against production: no email is sent. It does, however, consume rate-limit quota, because the check runs inside the router, after the limiter.

request.description:
The limiter allows 5 requests per IP per 15 minutes.

To trigger it, open the Collection Runner, select this request, set Iterations to 6 or more, and run. The first five pass validation; the sixth returns `429` with `RateLimit-*` headers.

The limiter is in-memory, so restarting the backend clears the counter. This payload is valid, so against a configured backend the first five iterations send real email - prefer running it locally with the mailer unconfigured.

item.name: CORS
item.description: Browser-origin allow-list behaviour. These send an `Origin` header explicitly, which Postman otherwise omits.

item.name: OPTIONS /api/contact - Preflight from an allowed origin

exec: pm.test('advertises the permitted methods and caches the preflight', () => {

request.description:
Simulates the browser preflight the site itself sends.

`http://localhost:5173` is on the built-in allow-list, so the response echoes the origin, advertises `GET, POST, OPTIONS`, and caches the preflight for 24 hours.

item.name: OPTIONS /api/contact - Preflight from a disallowed origin

exec: pm.test('does not leak a server error', () => {

request.description:
An origin that is not on the allow-list.

The API does **not** answer with an error status. It simply omits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and the browser blocks the response client-side. Throwing inside the origin callback would surface as a `500` and advertise that an allow-list exists, so the status is deliberately not asserted here - the missing header is the whole contract.

Note that CORS is a browser control, not authentication: Postman and curl send no `Origin` header and are unaffected, which is why the rest of this collection works against production.
Any unmatched path falls through to the catch-all handler, which returns `{ "success": false, "error": "Not found." }`.
